narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 61.8% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Your rejection was driven primarily by three pieces of information, ranked by importance. The strongest factor was your third-year class ranking, which placed you in the second decile. This was substantially lower than the average of accepted students (around the sixth decile) and strongly pushed the model toward predicting failure. Your first-year ranking in the third decile also worked against you, though with less force, again falling well below the typical performance of accepted applicants.

Your LSAT score of 35.5 worked in the opposite direction. While slightly below the accepted average of 37.2, it still provided a meaningful pull toward a passing outcome. However, this positive influence was not large enough to overcome the negative effect of your class rankings.

Taken together, the model concluded that your academic performance trajectory in law school made success on the bar exam less likely than the average applicant.

What you should do next is straightforward: focus on strengthening your academic record and consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score. Improving either of these areas, especially your class standing, would significantly improve your chances in a future application.
